proposal.title: Scalp-proof concert tickets as Bitcoin signet tokens for campus club events

proposal.problem: The music club organises three to four concerts a term in a hall of about 300 seats, and sells tickets through Instagram messages, bank transfers and a shared spreadsheet. A ticket is a QR code image sent by message, so anyone can screenshot and forward it: at the last spring concert the gate team found about 40 duplicated QR codes, and the people who arrived first got in while the real buyers were turned away. Popular concerts sell out in hours and tickets then reappear in WhatsApp groups at two to three times the price, which the club cannot stop and students blame on the club. Checking names against the spreadsheet at the door takes about 30 seconds per person, so queues reach 45 minutes and the concert starts late. Students who cannot attend have no safe way to pass their ticket to a friend, and after the event nothing remains of having been there, although many students collect tickets and wristbands as souvenirs.
proposal.mission: Give the Event organiser a way to issue every concert ticket as a token on the Bitcoin signet whose transfers the club co-signs only at face value, so that a Ticket holder can safely pass a ticket to a friend and keep it as a souvenir, and Gate staff can admit only the phone that holds the ticket.
proposal.outcome: At the door the gate staff scan a phone and see within two seconds whether its owner holds an unused ticket; screenshots and copies fail, resales above face value cannot be co-signed, and after the concert every attendee keeps the ticket in their collection as proof of having been there.

proposal.techWhy: schema.org already defines MusicEvent, Offer and Ticket, so events and tickets are standard linked data that search engines and calendars understand. Records are served as JSON-LD to the wallet and handled in Python with RDFLib. SHACL shapes, run with pySHACL, refuse an event without capacity or with a resale cap above face value, and the transfer service checks every resale against the same shapes. Oxigraph stores events, tickets and check-ins and answers SPARQL queries for a holder's souvenir collection. PROV-O records who issued and who moved each ticket, stable IRIs give every ticket a permanent page, and the KVKK regime keeps names off the chain.

proposal.spec: The system lets the event organiser create a concert as schema.org linked data with a capacity, a face value and resale rules, validated by SHACL shapes. For each ticket it mints a signet output locked by a script that needs both the holder's key and the club's key, or the holder's key alone after a time lock that ends a week after the event. The holder keeps the key in a phone wallet. A transfer is a transaction the holder signs and the club's service co-signs only when the confirmed price is at or below face value and the ticket has moved fewer than three times. At the door the scanner shows a fresh challenge, the wallet signs it with the holder's key, and the scanner admits the ticket if that key holds the unspent ticket output and it has not been checked in. After the time lock the ticket stays in the holder's collection as a souvenir.

scenarios.text: Given a holder whose phone wallet holds an unused ticket, when the gate staff scan the phone and the wallet signs the challenge, then the scanner shows a green result within two seconds and records the check-in
Given a screenshot of another person's ticket shown on a second phone, when the gate staff scan it, then the challenge signature fails and the scanner shows a red result naming the reason
Given a resale request at twice the face value, when the holder asks the club to co-sign the transfer, then the service refuses and the ticket stays with the holder
Given a ticket that has already moved three times, when its holder asks for a fourth transfer, then the service refuses and explains the limit

proposal.activity: The organiser creates an event; the shapes check it and refuse it with reasons if the capacity, the face value or the resale rules are missing or wrong. The organiser then mints the tickets: the service builds one signet transaction with one ticket output per ticket and records each ticket's outpoint. When a buyer has paid, the organiser assigns a ticket to the buyer's wallet key. A holder who cannot attend starts a transfer, both sides confirm the price, and the service co-signs if the rules allow. At the door the scanner challenges each wallet and records the check-in.
proposal.sequence: The organiser's page posts the event to the ticket service, which validates it with pySHACL and stores it in Oxigraph. To mint, the service asks the Bitcoin Core signet node to fund and sign a transaction from the club's wallet and stores the outpoints. For a transfer the wallet builds a PSBT spending the ticket output to a new script with the buyer's key, signs it and sends it to the service; the service checks the rules, adds the club's signature and a fee input, and broadcasts. At the door the scanner sends a nonce, the wallet returns a signature, and the scanner asks the service whether that key holds the unspent ticket output and whether it is already checked in.

proposal.classModel: Event is a schema:MusicEvent with a date, a venue, a capacity and a ResaleRule holding the face value, the price cap and the maximum number of transfers. Ticket is a schema:Ticket for one Event, identified by its mint outpoint, and is a prov:Entity. TicketOutput holds the current outpoint, the holder's public key and the script. Transfer is a prov:Activity linking the old and new TicketOutput, with the confirmed price and the club's co-signature. CheckIn links a Ticket to the time and the gate device. A Ticket has exactly one unspent TicketOutput at a time.

proposal.model_Data: Design-level class diagram: Event (schema:MusicEvent) with ResaleRule; Ticket (schema:Ticket, prov:Entity) for one Event; TicketOutput with outpoint, holder key and script; Transfer (prov:Activity) between outputs; CheckIn; shapes EventShape, ResaleRuleShape and TransferShape guard them.
proposal.model_Architecture: Deployment view: one Python ticket service with Oxigraph embedded and the club's co-signing key, one Bitcoin Core signet node reached over RPC, and static web pages for organiser, wallet and scanner; node address and keys are configuration so the club can move the service.
proposal.model_Security: Ticket output script: either the holder's and the club's signatures together, or after a lock time one week past the event the holder's signature alone. State machine of a ticket: minted, assigned, transferred, checked in, souvenir; a check-in is accepted once, and a challenge nonce is never reused.
proposal.model_User_interface: Wallet: a card per ticket with event, date and status, a transfer button and a show-at-door button; scanner: one full-screen green or red result with the reason; both readable on a phone in a dark hall.
proposal.model_Interaction: Sequence at the door: scanner shows a QR with a fresh nonce; the holder's wallet scans it, signs it and shows its answer as a QR; the scanner reads it, asks the service and shows the result.
proposal.model_Interface: Component diagram: OrganiserPage, WalletApp and ScannerPage call the TicketAPI; TicketAPI uses Store (Oxigraph, SPARQL), RulesValidator (pySHACL) and ChainService, which talks to the Bitcoin Core signet node over RPC and holds the club's key.
proposal.chainDesign: Bitcoin signet with a Bitcoin Core node. Each ticket is a small P2WSH output whose script is: two signatures (holder and club) or, after an absolute lock time with OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, the holder's signature alone. A ticket's identity is the outpoint that minted it, and every transfer spends the ticket output into output 0 of a new transaction, so the ticket's history is the chain of spends, like a coloured coin. Transfers are built as PSBTs: the holder signs, the club checks the price rule and co-signs, and the club adds the fee input. A blockchain is needed because ownership must be provable by the holder's key alone, independently of the club's database, and the time lock guarantees that the holder fully owns the ticket as a souvenir after the event even if the club disappears.

risks.risk: Holders lose the phone or clear the browser and lose the key
risks.mitigation: backup words shown on first use; before the event the club can re-issue a lost ticket with the co-signed path and record the old one as void

risks.risk: Gate scanning is slow in a crowded hall with weak signal
risks.mitigation: scanner caches the unspent ticket set before doors open and verifies signatures offline, syncing check-ins later

risks.risk: People resell above face value and pay each other outside the system
risks.mitigation: transfer limit of three, transfer only via confirmed price, and the club's report shows unusual transfer chains

risks.risk: The signet faucet runs dry while minting hundreds of outputs
risks.mitigation: fund the club wallet early, use small outputs, and keep regtest for automated tests
